transcript.text: Sometimes when I open the dishwasher there's grey smelly water in the bottom even though it finished draining fine. Not every day though. Kitchen sink was replaced last month if that matters.

The sink being replaced last month matters a lot here. If the dishwasher drains fine but grey, smelly water turns up later, and only some days, the most likely cause is dirty water from the sink waste running back into the dishwasher. That usually happens when the drain hose is no longer routed properly after a plumbing change. Likely causes, most likely first:
1. Backflow from the sink. The drain hose should rise in a high loop up under the worktop before it drops down to the sink waste. If it was left lying low when the new sink went in, sink water can run back down it. This is most likely if a full sink is emptied or a washing machine drains into the same waste.
2. A slow or partly blocked sink waste or trap. If the new trap drains sluggishly, water backs up into the dishwasher hose.
3. A partly blocked filter or sump in the dishwasher holding dirty water.
4. Less likely, the non-return valve inside the machine sticking, so water creeps back in. One normal point: a cupful of clean water sitting under the filter is normal, because it keeps the seals wet. Grey, smelly water covering the base is not. Checks, simplest first:
1. Notice when it happens. If the grey water appears after the sink has been emptied or another appliance has drained, that points strongly to backflow from the plumbing.
2. Look at the drain hose under the sink (no need to switch anything off just to look). - Does it run up high, ideally clipped near the underside of the worktop, before going down to the spigot on the sink waste? - If it runs straight across low down, or droops below the trap, that is very likely your cause. Lifting and securing it in a high loop often fixes it.
3. Run the sink tap hard for a minute. If the sink drains slowly or gurgles, the trap or waste may be partly blocked or fitted with too shallow a fall. A plunger, or a word with whoever fitted the sink, would sort that.
4. Switch off and unplug the dishwasher, put a towel down and take out the lower rack. Twist out the filter, rinse it, and wipe any sludge out of the sump. - If it was full of grease and food, that explains the smell. A hot empty wash with dishwasher cleaner afterwards will freshen it up. If the hose is correctly looped, the sink drains freely and the filter is clean, but the water still comes back, the non-return valve becomes the main suspect. So, when you find the grey water, has
It seems to happen after I've drained the sink full of washing-up water. The filter is clean though, I checked it. I'll go and look at the hose under the sink now.

That timing is the giveaway. If grey water turns up only after you've let a full sink of washing-up water go, it's probably sink water surging back down the dishwasher's drain hose, not a fault inside the machine. With a clean filter and the dishwasher draining fine itself, the inside of the machine looks less likely. The sink change last month makes a plumbing routing issue the front runner. While you're under the sink, look for these: 1. Hose height. The drain hose should climb up high, ideally clipped close to the underside of the worktop, then drop down to the spigot on the sink waste. If it runs low or sags below the trap, a rush of sink water can run straight back into the dishwasher. Lift it into a high loop and secure it with a clip or cable tie. That alone usually cures it. 2. Where it connects. Check the hose goes onto the dishwasher spigot on the trap or waste, ideally one with a built-in non-return valve, and that the jubilee clip is tight. Some new sink wastes have a spigot that sits quite low. If yours does, a high loop matters even more. An under-sink plumber can also fit a spigot with a non-return valve. 3. How fast the sink drains. Fill the sink, pull the plug and watch. If it drains slowly or gurgles, the new trap may be partly blocked or have too little fall, so the water backs up into the dishwasher branch. A plunger may clear it. If it's a fitting problem, it's worth asking whoever fitted the sink to come back, as it should have been right from the start. Once you've sorted the hose, run a hot empty wash with dishwasher cleaner to get rid of the smell left by the dirty water. If the hose is properly looped, the sink drains freely, and you still get grey water after draining the sink, the dishwasher's own non-return valve becomes the likely part. That's usually an engineer job to confirm and replace. What does the hose look like when you get under there?
Had a look. Since the new sink went in, the hose just lies on the cupboard floor and goes straight into the waste spigot, no high loop at all. The sink also drains a little slowly.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. That's probably your answer. When a full sink of washing-up water rushes down, some of it takes the easy route back along the hose into the dishwasher. A slightly slow sink makes that worse, because water backs up in the waste for longer. The dishwasher itself drains fine and the filter is clean, so I'm fairly confident the machine isn't faulty. 1. Lift the drain hose into a high loop. Raise it so it rises as high as it will go, ideally up near the underside of the worktop, then drops down to the spigot. Hold it there with a plastic clip, a cup hook or a cable tie fixed to the cabinet side. Don't pull it so tight that it kinks. If the hose won't stretch that far, even a loop well above the trap and spigot helps. You may need to ease the machine forward slightly to free up some slack.
2. Sort the slow sink. Put a bowl and towel under the trap, unscrew the bottle or U-bend, and clear any fat, food or fitting debris. Look into the dishwasher spigot on the waste too, in case it's partly clogged. Refit it hand-tight and run the tap to check for leaks. If it still drains slowly with the trap clean, the new waste may not have enough fall, which is worth raising with whoever fitted the sink.
3. Freshen it up. Run a hot empty wash with dishwasher cleaner to clear the smell left by the dirty water.
4. Test it. Fill the sink, pull the plug, then check the bottom of the dishwasher. If the hose can't be looped properly, a plumber can fit a waste spigot with a built-in non-return valve, which stops sink water getting into the hose at all. If grey water still appears after all that, the dishwasher's own non-return valve becomes the likely culprit. That would be an engineer job to confirm. Let me know how the test goes.
Right, I've looped the hose up high and clipped it under the worktop. I'll leave it a few days and see, but so far there's been no more water after draining the sink.

That's a good sign. No grey water after draining the sink is exactly what you'd expect if the missing high loop was the cause, so I'm confident that was it. Keeping an eye on it for a few days is sensible. To stop it coming back:
1. Clear the slow sink. If you haven't already, clean out the trap and the dishwasher spigot on the waste. A sluggish waste lets water sit and back up, and a free-flowing one takes the pressure off the hose.
2. Freshen the dishwasher. Run one hot empty wash with dishwasher cleaner to clear any smell left by the dirty water.
3. Keep the loop in place. If anyone works under the sink in future, make sure the hose stays clipped up high. If grey water ever comes back with the loop in place and the sink draining freely, the dishwasher's own non-return valve would be the next suspect. That's an engineer job to confirm. Is there anything else I can help with?
